query: For a damaged high-value component made from a material whose physical and microstructural characteristics make traditional fusion-welding repair ineffective because of hot-cracking risk, what intervention could enable continued service without replacing the entire part under aggressive operating conditions? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to traditional fusion-welding repair, the relevant operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.intervention: Apply friction stir processing (FSP) locally over the damaged region to repair the surface damage in the solid state, immediately followed by a controlled re-aging heat treatment to re‐precipitate the strengthening phases that may have been dissolved or coarsened during stirring.
generation.conditions: The intervention is conducted under parameters that keep processing temperatures below the melting point (thus avoiding formation of a liquid phase) and then subject the repaired zone to a re-aging heat treatment that is optimized for Inconel 713C. The final repaired component must reliably perform under aggressive high-temperature service conditions (around 700 °C) with cyclic mechanical loads.
generation.structural_mediator: The friction stir process promotes dynamic recrystallization and mechanical consolidation without reaching the high-temperature brittleness range (HTBR), while the subsequent re-aging treatment facilitates the re-formation of fine γ′/γ″ precipitates that are crucial for high-temperature strength.
generation.mechanism: Solid-state stirring repairs the defect zone without inducing a molten pool and eliminating the interdendritic liquid films responsible for hot cracking. However, FSP can potentially modify or partially dissolve the strengthening precipitates; the carefully controlled re-aging step after processing is designed to restore the original precipitation state, thereby maintaining the alloy’s high-temperature properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The repaired zone will show a refined, defect-free microstructure with re-established precipitation hardening, resulting in superior crack resistance and fatigue/creep performance compared to traditional fusion welding repairs that expose the material to prolonged HTBR conditions.
generation.baseline: Traditional fusion welding (TIG remelting/pad welding) of Inconel 713C that entails exposure to high temperatures in the HTBR, leading to partial melting, interdendritic liquid film formation, and the initiation of hot cracks.
generation.boundary: The combined FSP and re-aging repair must sustain integrity under service temperatures up to ~700 °C and fatigue loads typical of aircraft engine components. paper_did: Processed AA6061‐T6 sheets (3 mm thick) using multi‐pass friction stir processing (FSP) as a pre‐weld treatment to modify the base metal microstructure.
Performed bead‐on‐plate TIG fusion welding on both untreated and FSP‐treated specimens under controlled parameters.
Characterized the microstructure using optical microscopy, SEM, and EBSD—including measurements of grain size and dendrite arm spacing in the fusion zone (FZ) and heat affected zone (HAZ).
Conducted mechanical testing (tensile tests in both as‐weld and T6 heat‐treated conditions) to assess joint efficiency and overall weld quality.
paper_reported: FSP pre‐weld treatment refined the base metal microstructure, reducing the average grain size and dendrite arm spacing in the weld’s fusion zone.

The FSP‐treated welds exhibited dramatic mitigation of solidification cracking—both macro‐ and micro‐scale—with the refined grain structure promoting improved epitaxial growth and strain accommodation.

After post‐weld T6 heat treatment, the FSP‐treated welds achieved a joint efficiency of 0.95 relative to the base material, outperforming traditional fusion welding and even solid‐state friction stir welding.
paper_proposed: The study suggests that FSP as a pre‐weld treatment is a transformative approach to overcome hot cracking in AA6061, enabling its use in high‐integrity, lightweight structural applications.

It implicitly points to the need for further improvements—such as complete elimination of residual micro‐cracks and even finer microstructural control—to optimize ductility and performance in the weld zone.

paper_did: Conducted TIG remelting and pad-welding experiments on precision castings of Inconel 713C using two gas shield variants (pure argon and TecLine 8910 gas mixture).
Applied controlled variations in welding linear energy (e.g., below 0.17 kJ/mm to above 0.3 kJ/mm) and performed transvarestraint tests to impose deformation and quantify hot cracking susceptibility.

Measured key parameters such as the high‐temperature brittleness range (HTBR from approximately 1053 °C to 1299 °C), critical strain rate for temperature drop (0.0055 1/°C), critical strain speed (1.71 1/s), and identified a maximum allowable strain (εp) of 0.3% before cracking initiates.
paper_reported: Hot cracking in Inconel 713C during repair welding is primarily linked to the formation and rupture of interdendritic liquid films and the partial melting of dendrite boundaries and primary carbides in the HTBR.

Quantitative hot‐cracking criteria (including CST and CSS parameters) were determined to guide process parameters for repairing precision castings with minimal cracking.
paper_proposed: The paper suggests that the established technological guidelines and hot‐cracking criteria can serve as a basis for developing repair techniques or surface modification processes for Inconel 713C castings using controlled welding methods.

paper_did: Employed laser cladding to deposit nickel‐based transition layers (Inconel 718, Inconel 625, Hastelloy X, FGH4096, and FGH4169) onto H13 hot‐work die steel substrates, followed by a CoCrFeNiAl high‐entropy alloy working layer.

paper_reported: In the three‐point bending tests, Inconel 718 transition layers exhibited no interface cracks and provided excellent bond strength, whereas FGH4096, FGH4169, Inconel 625, and Hastelloy X showed cracking due to insufficient element diffusion or weak interfacial bonding.

It implies that further process optimization and exploration of transition layer design could extend the service life of components in high-temperature and cyclic load environments.

paper_did: Developed and implemented a multiple preheating process for EB‐PBF fabrication of IN738LC that minimizes temperature drops during printing.
Utilized a dual‐band infrared thermometer to monitor real‑time surface temperature variations during powder spreading, preheating, and forming.
Fabricated samples at different preheating temperatures (1000 °C, 1030 °C, and 1060 °C) to study the trade‐off between crack suppression and powder sintering/recyclability.
Conducted extensive microstructural characterization (OM, SEM, EDS, EBSD, TEM, EPMA, FIB) to identify the formation of low‐melting eutectics, carbides, and borides at grain boundaries.

High-temperature creep tests showed excellent endurance (lifetimes ranging from 53 to 69.25 hours) and revealed dynamic recrystallization that contributes to improved mechanical performance.
paper_proposed: Optimizing process parameters and further adjusting the preheating process to finely control temperature fluctuations during EB-PBF.

paper_did: Fabricated Hastelloy-X specimens using selective laser melting with two compositions: one without yttrium (HX) and one with 0.12 mass% yttrium (HX-a).
Applied a standard solution heat treatment (1177 °C for 2 h with air cooling) to both as‐built and heat-treated specimens.
Performed extensive microstructural characterization (using optical microscopy, SEM, EDS, FE-SEM, and EBSD) and conducted creep tests at 900 °C/80 MPa in both vertical and horizontal orientations.
paper_reported: Yttrium addition increased the hot cracking tendency (crack fraction increased from 1% in HX to 5% in HX-a) due to segregation of Y and formation of yttrium-rich carbides, yet improved creep performance by forming stable Y2O3 and SiO2 oxides inside the grains.

The improved creep life and ductility in the Y-added specimens were attributed to the discrete carbide precipitation at grain boundaries that promoted grain boundary pinning and the retention of a columnar grain morphology after heat treatment.
Anisotropic creep behavior was observed, with vertical specimens (aligned with the columnar grains) showing significantly enhanced creep life compared to horizontally oriented specimens.
paper_proposed: The study did not explicitly propose further future work; however, its findings imply that further optimization of alloying elements (such as yttrium) and processing (heat treatment) to balance hot cracking and creep resistance may be beneficial.

Prepared specimens by machining grooves in a copper plate, filling them with HEA particles (at 5, 10, and 15 vol%), compacting the particles, and then undertaking FSP with a rotating tool (1000 rpm, 30 mm/min traverse).

fields.hypothesis: Integrating a nanoparticle pre-deposition with friction stir processing (FSP) can further refine the repair zone's microstructure, reducing dendrite arm spacing and enhancing crack resistance beyond that of FSP alone under aggressive conditions.

fields.conditions: The repair is implemented under aggressive operating conditions characterized by high cyclic stresses and temperature fluctuations; the nanoparticle layer must be uniformly applied and integrated during FSP.
fields.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained, nanoparticle-reinforced stir zone with reduced primary dendrite arm spacing.
fields.mechanism: The nanoparticles act as heterogeneous nucleation sites during FSP-induced dynamic recrystallization, leading to even finer grain formation and a further reduction in dendrite arm spacing. This lowers the cracking-susceptibility index by improving grain boundary strength and strain accommodation, as suggested by both the paper’s discussion on nanoparticle additions and established precipitation hardening principles.

fields.boundary: Success depends on achieving uniform nanoparticle dispersion and integration; the method is suitable for repair regions where surface preparation permits nanoparticle adherence.
fields.uncertainty: While the role of nanoparticles in mitigating cracking is known, the magnitude of improvement in a repair context under in-service aggressive conditions is less documented and must be quantified.

fields.hypothesis: Employ friction stir repair combined with an in situ post-process re-aging treatment to restore the precipitation-hardened microstructure, thereby achieving a solid‐state repair that avoids fusion‐welding hot cracking while preserving high‐temperature mechanical properties.
fields.material_initial_state: A high‐value Inconel 713C component produced by precision casting, with a microstructure containing dendritic γ matrix, strengthening precipitates (γ′/γ″), and carbide constituents prone to hot cracking when exposed to fusion temperatures.
fields.intervention: Apply friction stir processing (FSP) locally over the damaged region to repair the surface damage in the solid state, immediately followed by a controlled re-aging heat treatment to re‐precipitate the strengthening phases that may have been dissolved or coarsened during stirring.
fields.conditions: The intervention is conducted under parameters that keep processing temperatures below the melting point (thus avoiding formation of a liquid phase) and then subject the repaired zone to a re-aging heat treatment that is optimized for Inconel 713C. The final repaired component must reliably perform under aggressive high-temperature service conditions (around 700 °C) with cyclic mechanical loads.
fields.structural_mediator: The friction stir process promotes dynamic recrystallization and mechanical consolidation without reaching the high-temperature brittleness range (HTBR), while the subsequent re-aging treatment facilitates the re-formation of fine γ′/γ″ precipitates that are crucial for high-temperature strength.
fields.mechanism: Solid-state stirring repairs the defect zone without inducing a molten pool and eliminating the interdendritic liquid films responsible for hot cracking. However, FSP can potentially modify or partially dissolve the strengthening precipitates; the carefully controlled re-aging step after processing is designed to restore the original precipitation state, thereby maintaining the alloy’s high-temperature properties.
fields.predicted_outcome: The repaired zone will show a refined, defect-free microstructure with re-established precipitation hardening, resulting in superior crack resistance and fatigue/creep performance compared to traditional fusion welding repairs that expose the material to prolonged HTBR conditions.
fields.baseline: Traditional fusion welding (TIG remelting/pad welding) of Inconel 713C that entails exposure to high temperatures in the HTBR, leading to partial melting, interdendritic liquid film formation, and the initiation of hot cracks.
fields.boundary: The combined FSP and re-aging repair must sustain integrity under service temperatures up to ~700 °C and fatigue loads typical of aircraft engine components. The process parameters (tool rotational speed, traverse speed, and re-aging temperature/time) must be optimized to balance recrystallization with precipitation restoration.
fields.uncertainty: While the mechanism is sound based on solid-state processing principles, the exact re-aging parameters needed to fully restore the original precipitation strengthening and quantify fatigue/creep improvements require experimental calibration.

fields.hypothesis: Utilize a solid-state cold spray deposition method to apply an HEA-based overlay for repairing the damaged component, avoiding fusion-related hot-cracking while imparting superior surface properties.
fields.material_initial_state: A high-value component with a microstructure that precludes effective fusion-weld repairs due to hot-cracking risks.
fields.intervention: Mechanically prepare and clean the surface, then cold spray an HEA powder (for instance, AlCoCrCuFe or an alternative HEA with high toughness) onto the damaged area to form a protective and structurally integrated overlay.
fields.conditions: The cold spray process should be optimized to achieve high particle velocity and good interfacial bonding at ambient or moderately elevated temperatures, ensuring a dense coating. The repaired component must remain operational under high mechanical loads, elevated contact stresses, and thermal cycling.
fields.structural_mediator: A dense, well-adhered HEA overlay with a microstructure characterized by work-induced deformation and minimal thermal damage, promoting compressive residual stresses and strong bonding with the base metal.
fields.mechanism: Cold spraying is a solid-state process that accelerates HEA powder particles against the substrate, bonding them through severe plastic deformation without melting. This avoids the formation of fusion-induced hot cracks. The resultant overlay provides enhanced hardness, wear resistance, and a gradient interface that dissipates stresses.
fields.predicted_outcome: The cold-sprayed repair overlay is anticipated to show superior resistance to wear and cracking compared to conventional fusion-weld repairs, with a lower risk of hot cracking due to absence of melting and reduced thermal stresses.
fields.baseline: Traditional fusion-based welding repairs result in hot cracking due to high heat input, making them unsuitable for the given component.
fields.boundary: If the cold spray parameters are poorly controlled, the coating might exhibit insufficient adhesion or porosity, compromising performance; additionally, the overlay thickness and interface gradient must be optimized for aggressive service conditions.
fields.uncertainty: Though cold spray is a proven repair technique, the exact improvement in service life relative to fusion repairs under the specific operating conditions is uncertain without experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare damaged components repaired via the cold spray deposition of an HEA overlay and compare them to components repaired using traditional fusion welding. Subject both groups to identical mechanical stress, thermal cycling, and tribological wear tests.
measurements: Adhesion strength analysis (pull-off or scratch tests)
Microstructural examination (porosity, bonding interface quality via SEM)
Fatigue and wear performance under cyclic loading
Measurement of residual stress profiles (using X-ray diffraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cold-sprayed overlays exhibit inferior adhesion, higher porosity, or do not demonstrate improved crack resistance and wear performance compared to fusion-weld repairs under aggressive conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.what_is_new: It proposes a localized, spot-based repair method that couples friction stir processing with mechanical surface peening—offering a new strategy to repair high-value components by mitigating hot cracking and enhancing local fatigue life without full fusion welding.

fields.hypothesis: Implement a friction stir spot repair (FSSR) combined with localized surface peening to induce compressive residual stresses and a refined microstructure in the damaged area, thereby enhancing crack resistance and service performance.
fields.material_initial_state: A damaged high-value component where conventional fusion welding leads to hot cracking due to unfavorable thermal and microstructural characteristics.
fields.intervention: Apply a friction stir spot repair technique focused on the damaged region with a specially designed tool that not only induces plastic deformation but also performs controlled surface peening. Optional addition of a minor HEA particulate reinforcement can be used to further augment the wear properties.
fields.conditions: The process is to be implemented at a rotational speed and traverse pattern that ensures localized severe plastic deformation without reaching melting temperatures, suitable for components operating under high cyclic loads and frictional contacts.
fields.structural_mediator: A localized spot with an ultrafine, recrystallized microstructure, embedded with compressive residual stresses and, if used, uniformly distributed fine HEA particles that act as crack arrestors.
fields.mechanism: Friction stir spot repair entails a solid-state modification that induces significant grain refinement and compressive residual stresses. When combined with surface peening, the near-surface tensile stresses are transformed into beneficial compressive stresses that delay crack initiation and propagation. The potential incorporation of fine HEA particles adds local hardness and improves load transfer, which further inhibits crack growth.
fields.predicted_outcome: The repaired spot is expected to exhibit significantly enhanced fatigue and wear resistance compared to traditional fusion-weld repairs, with a marked reduction in hot cracking; improved service performance is predicted under aggressive cyclic and thermal loading.
fields.baseline: Traditional fusion welding repairs produce high tensile stresses and hot cracking, which compromise the part under cyclic and thermal aggressive conditions.
fields.boundary: The process window requires careful parameter control; if the induced plastic deformation is insufficient or excessive, or if surface peening is not uniform, the benefits (i.e., compressive residual stress and crack arresting) may not materialize.
fields.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvements are supported by solid-state principles and FSP literature, the precise extent of fatigue life extension under specific service conditions remains to be quantified.

top3.label: C2
top3.builds_on: The finding that hot cracking in Inconel 713C occurs due to liquid-phase formation during fusion welding (PMC8778835) and that avoiding the high-temperature brittleness range prevents these defects.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes to combine a solid-state friction stir repair with a subsequent re-aging treatment specifically designed to restore the critical precipitation-hardened microstructure, addressing the shortcoming of friction stir processing that might otherwise degrade high-temperature performance.

fields.hypothesis: Employ friction stir repair combined with an in situ post-process re-aging treatment to restore the precipitation-hardened microstructure, thereby achieving a solid‐state repair that avoids fusion‐welding hot cracking while preserving high‐temperature mechanical properties.
fields.material_initial_state: A high‐value Inconel 713C component produced by precision casting, with a microstructure containing dendritic γ matrix, strengthening precipitates (γ′/γ″), and carbide constituents prone to hot cracking when exposed to fusion temperatures.
fields.intervention: Apply friction stir processing (FSP) locally over the damaged region to repair the surface damage in the solid state, immediately followed by a controlled re-aging heat treatment to re‐precipitate the strengthening phases that may have been dissolved or coarsened during stirring.
fields.conditions: The intervention is conducted under parameters that keep processing temperatures below the melting point (thus avoiding formation of a liquid phase) and then subject the repaired zone to a re-aging heat treatment that is optimized for Inconel 713C. The final repaired component must reliably perform under aggressive high-temperature service conditions (around 700 °C) with cyclic mechanical loads.
fields.structural_mediator: The friction stir process promotes dynamic recrystallization and mechanical consolidation without reaching the high-temperature brittleness range (HTBR), while the subsequent re-aging treatment facilitates the re-formation of fine γ′/γ″ precipitates that are crucial for high-temperature strength.
fields.mechanism: Solid-state stirring repairs the defect zone without inducing a molten pool and eliminating the interdendritic liquid films responsible for hot cracking. However, FSP can potentially modify or partially dissolve the strengthening precipitates; the carefully controlled re-aging step after processing is designed to restore the original precipitation state, thereby maintaining the alloy’s high-temperature properties.
fields.predicted_outcome: The repaired zone will show a refined, defect-free microstructure with re-established precipitation hardening, resulting in superior crack resistance and fatigue/creep performance compared to traditional fusion welding repairs that expose the material to prolonged HTBR conditions.
fields.baseline: Traditional fusion welding (TIG remelting/pad welding) of Inconel 713C that entails exposure to high temperatures in the HTBR, leading to partial melting, interdendritic liquid film formation, and the initiation of hot cracks.
fields.boundary: The combined FSP and re-aging repair must sustain integrity under service temperatures up to ~700 °C and fatigue loads typical of aircraft engine components. The process parameters (tool rotational speed, traverse speed, and re-aging temperature/time) must be optimized to balance recrystallization with precipitation restoration.
fields.uncertainty: While the mechanism is sound based on solid-state processing principles, the exact re-aging parameters needed to fully restore the original precipitation strengthening and quantify fatigue/creep improvements require experimental calibration.

Repair half using traditional fusion-weld repair and half using the proposed friction stir repair followed by re-aging. falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the friction stir plus re-aging specimens do not demonstrate statistically significant microstructural refinement, restoration of precipitation phases, and enhanced fatigue/creep performance compared to the fusion-welded specimens, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.builds_on: the finding that slow cooling can promote γ′ precipitate coarsening and induce beneficial serrated grain boundaries (PMC9848264::web::017::discussion)
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes combining a mechanical repair process (FSP) with a tailored subsequent heat treatment to overcome the limitations of fusion welding for high-value components, ensuring that sufficient precipitate coarsening occurs to generate serrated boundaries.

fields.hypothesis: Integrate friction stir processing with an immediate post-FSP solution and slow-cooling heat treatment to induce serrated grain boundaries in the damaged region.
fields.material_initial_state: A high-value component with localized damage characterized by coarse, straight grain boundaries and absence of beneficial precipitate structures that impede intergranular cracking.
fields.intervention: Apply friction stir processing (FSP) locally over the damaged zone to induce dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement. Immediately afterwards, subject the FSP‐treated region to a high-temperature solution heat treatment (e.g., 1120°C for 1 h, above the γ′ solvus) followed by a slow cooling at ~1°C/min down to ~1000°C, and finally, perform an aging treatment.
fields.conditions: Processing is carried out in situ under an inert atmosphere where necessary. The heat treatment cycle is closely controlled to mimic the slow-cooling conditions that produce coarse γ′ precipitates. The repaired part is then tested for high-temperature performance at around 650°C under tensile and creep loads.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of coarse γ′ precipitates along mobile grain boundaries during slow cooling, which pin the boundaries and force them into a serrated morphology.
fields.mechanism: FSP induces severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization generating fine equiaxed grains. The subsequent solution treatment dissolves any existing precipitates, and controlled slow cooling allows for the coarsening of γ′ precipitates. These coarse precipitates interact with the migrating grain boundaries and induce a serrated morphology that more evenly distributes local strains and resists intergranular crack propagation, similar to the mechanism reported in PMC9848264::web::017::discussion.
fields.predicted_outcome: The repaired region is expected to exhibit significantly improved high-temperature tensile ductility and a markedly extended creep rupture life relative to traditional fusion-weld repairs with straight grain boundaries. The improvements may approach the previously observed magnitudes (e.g., up to ~3.5 times increased ductility and a 400-fold increase in creep life) though quantitative gains are uncertain.
fields.baseline: Traditional fusion welding repair, which produces homogenously straight grain boundaries prone to hot-cracking and limited ductility at elevated temperatures.
fields.boundary: Aggressive operating conditions at around 650°C under high mechanical loading.
fields.uncertainty: While the qualitative benefits of serrated grain boundaries are well supported, the exact quantitative improvements depend on optimizing FSP parameters and the post-treatment heat cycle.

top3.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that prolonged exposure in the HTBR leads to interdendritic cracking (PMC8778835) and integrates advanced surface engineering techniques to minimize thermal input while achieving effective repair.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis innovates by combining high-velocity arc spraying with ultra-short pulse laser processing to achieve a minimally molten repair overlay, thus drastically reducing time in the critical HTBR and preventing hot cracking—a strategy not previously explored in the literature for Inconel 713C repair.

fields.hypothesis: Adopt a hybrid repair approach combining high-velocity arc spraying to deposit a pre-alloyed powder layer followed by ultra-short pulse laser processing to locally fuse the overlay without bulk remelting, thus minimizing time in the high-temperature brittleness range (HTBR).
fields.material_initial_state: A critically damaged Inconel 713C component where traditional fusion welding creates extensive partially melted zones leading to pervasive hot cracking due to the alloy’s wide HTBR and elemental segregation.
fields.intervention: First, apply high-velocity arc spraying to deposit a thin, pre-alloyed, low-cracking-potential powder overlay that has been specially formulated to mitigate segregation effects. Then, use an ultra-short (femtosecond to picosecond) pulse laser to selectively remelt only the very top surface of the deposit at extremely low heat input, ensuring rapid solidification.
fields.conditions: The process must be performed under controlled atmospheric conditions to avoid oxidation, and the ultra-short pulse laser parameters must be optimized to achieve only superficial fusion. The resulting repaired layer must operate reliably under aggressive service conditions (up to ~700 °C) with minimal thermal distortion.
fields.structural_mediator: The initial high-velocity arc spray creates a dense, adherent overlay with a controlled composition that already minimizes segregation. The ultra-short laser pulse then fuses the surface within microseconds, significantly reducing the time available for the material to dwell in the HTBR and preventing the formation of detrimental interdendritic liquid films.
fields.mechanism: By limiting the extent and duration of melting to only a superficial layer, the hybrid approach minimizes exposure to temperatures where hot cracking is prone to occur. The rapid re-solidification from the ultra-short pulse laser processing locks in a refined microstructure with minimal diffusion and segregation, thereby suppressing crack initiation mechanisms associated with conventional fusion welding.
fields.predicted_outcome: The repaired region will possess a strong metallurgical bond to the substrate, a refined and crack-free microstructure in the overlay, and exhibit improved resistance to hot cracking as well as enhanced high-temperature mechanical performance when compared to conventional fusion-weld repairs.
fields.baseline: Conventional fusion-welding repair that subjects the entire cross-sectional area of the repair to prolonged high-temperature exposure, leading to extensive partially melted zones and hot cracking.
fields.boundary: The overlay and its fusion layer must maintain mechanical integrity and metallurgical compatibility with the base material under service temperatures near 700 °C and during cyclic loading. The process must also avoid significant dilution of the substrate composition.
fields.uncertainty: The exact processing window—balancing sufficient surface melting against avoiding bulk remelting—and the optimized composition of the spray powder for best performance require detailed experimental tuning.
